description: To the infinity and beyond! - Buzz Lightyear
summary:
Astronaut Health Companion HARMONY is an offline-first health monitoring and decision-support application designed to help astronauts monitor their physical and psychological well-being during long-duration space missions. Built with Expo, React Native, Python, FastAPI, and MongoDB Atlas, the application runs on both mobile devices and laptops.

The application addresses NASA's five human spaceflight hazards through a simple daily health check-in, covering vital signs, mood, crew tension, symptoms, sleep, exercise, nutrition, hydration, and radiation exposure. It translates collected data into visual health indicators, personalized trends, alerts, and actionable guidance. Astronauts can also explore an interactive body visualization, monitor radiation readings, and generate health reports for flight surgeons.

Designed for the communication limitations of deep-space missions, the application stores information locally and synchronizes changes with the backend whenever connectivity becomes available.

This project is important because timely health awareness and early identification of potential problems are essential when immediate medical assistance from Earth is not possible. Through ensuring that health monitoring is accessible, understandable, and resilient to communication delays, HARMONY aims to support astronaut autonomy and crew health on future long-duration missions.
details:
What it does and how it works

Astronaut Health Companion Platform HARMONY is a self-assessment tool for astronauts on long missions, where a call to Mission Control can take many minutes each way. Each day the astronaut completes a three-minute check-in covering vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, optional blood sugar), mood and crew tension, symptoms, sleep, exercise, and food and fluids. Every step explains why we ask and how to measure it. The app compares each result with the astronaut’s own baseline and shows a color-coded status of Nominal, Watch or Action, always with a text label so color is never the only signal. It then gives plain-language guidance on what to do, and when to contact a flight surgeon. Trend charts show a personal normal range and a flag line, a tappable body view explains what spaceflight changes in each body area, and a radiation center tracks dose against NASA’s 600 mSv career limit. A flight surgeon report summarizes flags, indicators, symptoms and recommended actions, and can be queued for the next communication window or exported as text.

It works offline first. Everything is saved and evaluated on the device, and a small Python service syncs entries to MongoDB Atlas when the link is available. Only new items are sent, never the full history, and retries never create duplicates.

Benefits

Astronauts get an immediate, understandable answer about their health without waiting for ground support. Small drifts, such as three nights of short sleep, rising resting heart rate or falling mood, are caught early, before they become critical. The flight surgeon receives a short, structured summary instead of raw data, which suits limited bandwidth.

Intended impact

The project aims to make crews more independent and safer on missions to the Moon and Mars, where distance from Earth is one of NASA’s five spaceflight hazards. It also treats mental health and crew dynamics as seriously as physical vitals, and makes radiation exposure visible every day.

Tools, languages and software

  • Frontend: TypeScript, React Native with Expo and expo-router, React Native Web, react-native-svg, AsyncStorage
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, uvicorn, pymongo
  • Database: MongoDB Atlas, inspected with MongoDB Compass
  • Other: Git and GitHub, VS Code. No special hardware is needed. It runs on phones and on astronaut laptops through the browser.

What is creative about it

  • It is organized around NASA’s own five hazards and their health risks, not around generic fitness tracking.
  • The interface is designed for low bandwidth: system fonts, no images or video, icons drawn inline, and cached screens.
  • Rules and advice live in one JSON file on the server. Flight surgeons can tune thresholds and guidance without changing the app, and the app keeps a cached copy for offline use.
  • Status is judged against each astronaut’s own baseline, not only population ranges.
  • A solar particle event simulation, with a banner and a dose jump, shows how the app would react to a radiation emergency.

Factors the team considered

  • Connectivity: delayed and limited links led to the offline-first design, queued syncing and small payloads.
  • Safety and honesty: the app is decision support, not a diagnosis. Thresholds are clearly marked as placeholders for medical review, and only the radiation career limit, from NASA-STD-3001, is taken from an official source.
  • Usability: astronauts are not medical experts, so every measurement and indicator comes with simple instructions and explanations. The status colors are always paired with text and the tap targets are large.
  • Flexibility: requirements and official resources can change, so colors live in one theme file and limits in one rules file.
  • Scope: prioritizing the time frame of the Hackathon, we prioritized the daily check-in, trends, radiation and reporting over secondary features.

AI Acknowledgement

Claude was used as an AI-assisted development tool during the creation of Astronaut Health Companion. Its assistance covered portions of both the frontend and backend implementation, as well as technical documentation.

Specifically, AI assistance was used for:

Frontend development: Generating, refining, and debugging portions of the TypeScript and React Native code, including UI components, screen layouts, navigation, data handling, local storage, visualizations, and synchronization logic.

Health assessment and guidance configuration: Assisting with the structure, organization, wording, and formatting of the backend rules.json file, including indicator descriptions, threshold configurations, status explanations, and recommended actions.

Backend development: Assisting with portions of the Python and FastAPI implementation, including API endpoint structure, data synchronization, database interactions, and configuration.

Documentation: Helping draft and refine the README, setup instructions, architecture descriptions, and technical explanations.

Debugging and development support: Explaining errors, suggesting fixes, reviewing code changes, and helping improve consistency across the application.

AI-generated suggestions and code were not treated as automatically correct or production-ready. The development team reviewed and adapted AI-assisted outputs, integrated them into the existing project, and performed testing to verify application functionality and compatibility.

The development team retains responsibility for the final implementation, design decisions, code integration, and project deliverables. In particular, the health thresholds and guidance included in this prototype are not clinically validated medical recommendations. AI assistance does not constitute medical or scientific validation of the application's health assessment logic.
